issue: The conditions for using negative confirmations are stated incompletely in three places. The lesson takeaway and flashcard f3 leave out the requirement that the auditor has obtained evidence that the relevant controls operate effectively. The takeaway also says negative requests are "used only when" the conditions hold, but the conditions apply only when negative requests are the SOLE substantive procedure. The aud-ev-01 explanation says "AU-C 505 lists conditions that must all be present" but never lists them.
evidence: AU-C 505.15 allows negative requests as the sole substantive procedure only if all four hold: (a) RMM is assessed as low AND the auditor has obtained sufficient appropriate evidence about the operating effectiveness of the relevant controls; (b) a large number of small, homogeneous items; (c) a very low exception rate is expected; (d) the auditor knows of nothing that would make recipients disregard the requests. The lesson takeaway reads: "used only when RMM is low, there are many small, homogeneous balances, few exceptions are expected, and recipients are expected to read them". It omits the controls limb and implies negative requests can never supplement other procedures. Flashcard f3 has the same gap: "Low RMM, many small homogeneous balances, few exceptions expected, and recipients expected to read the requests." The same bank states the rule differently: aud-x3-33 (mock-2) explains "RMM is low and controls are effective ...". A student taught from this lesson would miss an exam option such as "the auditor has tested controls and found them effective".
source: AU-C 505.15 (AICPA, SAS 122 as amended); review/reference/aud-standards.md §9 (negative confirmations row)
fix: Lesson takeaway: "Negative requests may be the SOLE substantive procedure only if all four hold: (1) RMM is low and controls have been tested and found effective; (2) many small, homogeneous balances; (3) a very low exception rate is expected; (4) no reason to expect recipients to ignore them. Otherwise use them only together with other procedures." Use the same four conditions for the f3 back and in the aud-ev-01 item and key explanations.

issue: The lesson's AS 2310 (revised) section and aud-ev-12 say an issuer auditor may skip receivable confirmation by documenting why it "would not be feasible or effective". The "or effective" ground comes from the superseded interim AS 2310.34 and from AICPA AU-C 330.20. The 2023 standard allows other procedures only when confirmation, or direct access to a knowledgeable external source, is NOT FEASIBLE. The aud-ev-12 stem ("an auditor decides not to confirm") also implies a discretion the revised standard removed. The key (a) is still the best option, but the item explanation, both choice explanations and the lesson teach the old exception.
evidence: aud-ev-12 choice a explanation: "The auditor must document why confirmation would not be feasible or effective ..."; choice b: "... unless the auditor documents why it would not be feasible or effective." The lesson says the same. The PCAOB adopting release (Rel. 2023-008) and the SEC/Federal Register filings describe AS 2310.25 as follows. The auditor confirms accounts receivable or directly accesses a knowledgeable external source. Only if the auditor determines that this is not feasible does the auditor perform other substantive procedures, including tests of details that obtain external evidence indirectly (for example, subsequent cash receipts). The old grounds of "immaterial", "ineffective" or "low RMM" are gone. A web-search summary also reports a requirement to communicate to the audit committee when confirmation was not performed; that part is unverified. The AICPA wording appears, correctly, in aud-revenue-receivables (aud-rev-chk2, AU-C 330). Mixing the two frameworks here blurs the issuer versus nonissuer distinction that the exam tests.
source: PCAOB AS 2310 (Rel. 2023-008), effective for FYs ending on or after June 15, 2025: https://assets.pcaobus.org/pcaob-dev/docs/default-source/rulemaking/docket_028/2023-008_confirmation-adopting-release.pdf ; https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2023-10-17/html/2023-22491.htm ; review/reference/aud-standards.md §4 (AS 2310 row)
fix: Lesson bullet: "confirm cash held by third parties and accounts receivable (or directly access a knowledgeable external source); only if the auditor determines this is not feasible, perform other substantive procedures, including tests of details using externally sourced evidence such as subsequent cash receipts, and document the determination". Contrast it with AU-C 330, where "ineffective" is still a ground. aud-ev-12 stem: "... determines that confirming an issuer's receivables is not feasible. What is required?" Delete "or effective" from the explanations of choices a and b, and change the b trap to wrong-rule. Verify the audit committee communication requirement and add it if confirmed.

issue: Three items are labelled skill "evaluation" with difficulty 3, but each is one-rule recall or simple application with three implausible options. That is two levels too high, and it inflates the evaluation share that the Blueprint skill mix depends on.
evidence: aud-ev-15: the stem itself says the documents are of low quality ("weak controls over their preparation") and asks whether quantity makes them sufficient. The answer restates AU-C 500.A6, which is remembering. aud-ev-26 options: rely, ignore, withdraw, investigate. The only reasonable choice is "investigate", which is application at most. aud-ev-27: "inquiry alone is not sufficient for a significant risk" is a recall rule (AU-C 330.21). The Blueprint defines evaluation as examining or assessing problems and using judgment to draw conclusions. None of these needs that: no facts are weighed and no conclusion is drawn from evidence. The module's label counts (R13/A13/An6/E3) depend on these three items for its whole evaluation share.
source: AICPA 2026 Blueprint skill definitions (review/reference/blueprint-notes.md, AUD skill allocation)
fix: Relabel aud-ev-15 as remembering, difficulty 1, and aud-ev-26 and aud-ev-27 as application, difficulty 2. Alternatively, rewrite them as true evaluation cases. Example: give mixed evidence for one assertion and ask the candidate to conclude whether it is sufficient and appropriate and what is still needed, as the aud-tbs-u6-sufficiency rows do.

issue: Skill and difficulty labels are one level too high, and they are inconsistent across items that test the same rule. aud-ev-17, -19, -20, -24 and -25 are labelled analysis (difficulty 3 for -19, -20, -24 and -25), but each applies one rule to a described procedure, which is application. aud-ev-18 (pure recall of the 60-day period) is labelled application, although its twin aud-x3-42 is labelled remembering.
evidence: Tracing shipping documents to recorded sales tests completeness. That one fact carries four different labels: aud-ev-22 remembering/2, aud-x3-29 application/2, aud-ev-17 analysis/2 and aud-ev-24 analysis/3. aud-ev-20 (an oral confirmation response is not a confirmation) is a recall rule. aud-ev-19 (inconsistent evidence leads to modified procedures, AU-C 500.11) is a recall rule. aud-ev-25 (confirmations support valuation least) mirrors the lesson pre-question aud-ev-pre1, which is labelled remembering/2.
fix: Relabel aud-ev-17, -19, -20, -24 and -25 as application, difficulty 2, and aud-ev-18 as remembering, difficulty 1. Keep aud-ev-11 (analysis, difficulty 3) as the module's genuine analysis item.

issue: Several trap labels do not match the misconception the distractor models. "partial-computation" is used on non-numeric items. Direction-of-testing errors are labelled "wrong-classification" in some items and "reversed" in others. "outdated-rule" is used where no earlier rule ever said the thing.
evidence: partial-computation on items with no computation: aud-ev-17 c ("Accuracy only"), aud-ev-20 b ("Yes, if the auditor documents it"), aud-ev-23 c ("Cutoff only, at year-end"), aud-ev-27 d ("Only if controls are tested"). Vouching/tracing direction errors labelled wrong-classification: aud-ev-22 a ("That's vouching"), aud-ev-23 b ("That's tracing"), aud-ev-24 a ("That's vouching from the journal"). The same error is labelled "reversed" in aud-ev-16 a, aud-ev-17 a and aud-x3-29 b. aud-ev-12 b ("Nothing, since confirming is optional") is labelled outdated-rule, but under the interim AS 2310 confirming receivables was also presumptively required, so "optional" was never the rule.
fix: Use "reversed" for aud-ev-22 a, aud-ev-23 b and aud-ev-24 a. Use "overgeneralization" or "wrong-rule" for aud-ev-17 c, aud-ev-20 b, aud-ev-23 c and aud-ev-27 d. Use "wrong-rule" for aud-ev-12 b.

issue: Many distractor explanations are thin or circular and do not say why the option is wrong. In aud-ev-22 the reasoning given is actually wrong.
evidence: Examples: aud-ev-pre1 b "Not the primary purpose."; aud-ev-16 b and d "Not the main assertion."; aud-ev-17 b "Not tested this way."; aud-ev-18 c and aud-ev-20 d "That isn't what the rule says."; aud-ev-19 d "Not automatically."; aud-ev-21 a, b and d all "That evidence is less reliable."; aud-ev-22 b (Valuation) and c (Rights) "Not the direction." Valuation and rights are not direction-of-testing assertions, so "direction" does not explain why they are wrong. aud-ev-23 c "Not the main assertion." and d "Not the direction."; aud-ev-24 c and d "That is not what this tests."; aud-ev-25 b "They provide some evidence." and d "They give some support."; aud-ev-27 c "Still not enough."
fix: Give each distractor a one-line rule. Examples. aud-ev-22 b: "Valuation is tested by pricing and recalculation, not by tracing documents into the records." aud-ev-21 b: "Internal documents are reliable only to the extent the controls over their preparation are effective." aud-ev-25 d: "A confirmed balance implies the underlying sales occurred, so confirmations do give some occurrence evidence." aud-ev-19 d: "A disclaimer follows only if the inconsistency cannot be resolved and the possible effects are material and pervasive."
